AI is already embedded in supply chain planning and execution, but data quality and legacy systems remain major barriers to broader adoption, according to the 2027 Third-Party Logistics Study.

Released during the CSCMP EDGE conference, the annual study also examines strategic partnerships, supply chain resilience, freight fraud, and cargo theft. The study was founded by Dr. John Langley, emeritus professor at the University of Tennessee, and is supported by Penske Logistics and NTT Data.

Sixty-six percent of shippers surveyed said they use AI for predictive analytics and risk planning, compared with 43% of third-party logistics providers. 3PLs reported using AI for generative AI, machine learning, optimization, and autonomous decision-making.
Data quality and availability was the most common barrier to wider adoption, cited by 61% of respondents. Legacy system integration followed at 54%, while 46% cited budget constraints.

“The study shows data quality and legacy integration remain the top barriers to scaling AI, and that should be a wake-up call,” said Jonathan Whitaker, managing director, supply chain consulting, NTT Data Inc.

FORVIA HELLA has won the German Sustainability Award 2027 in the Products category. The award recognizes the “Circular One Eco Headlamp” concept. The company developed the sustainable headlamp concept as part of the publicly funded NALYSES consortium. Project partners included BMW Group, Covestro, geba, Miele, the Heinz Nixdorf Institute of Paderborn University and the Fraunhofer Institute for Mechatronic Design Engineering IEM. Hamm-Lippstadt University of Applied Sciences also participated.
The project’s results will inform the development of future headlamp generations and other products and applications.
FORVIA HELLA Headlamp Concept Focuses on Sustainability

The NALYSES research project concluded in June 2026 and resulted in the “One Circular Headlamp” concept. The project explored how manufacturers could design and produce future products with greater resource efficiency and lower emissions. Researchers used a headlamp as an example.
The German Sustainability Award 2027 recognizes the concept’s sustainable product design, material strategies, recycling options and use phase.

Compared with a conventional product, the headlamp concept can reduce CO2 emissions by approximately 50% over its entire life cycle. This includes materials, manufacturing, product use, reuse and recycling at the end of its service life.
Research Findings Could Shape Future Headlamp Design

“This award is an outstanding recognition of the commitment and joint efforts of everyone involved in the NALYSES consortium,” said Juan Manuel Mollà, managing director of lighting at FORVIA HELLA. “I would like to thank our team and project partners, whose expertise has helped generate important insights into more resource-efficient product design. The findings from the project make an important contribution to shaping future headlamp design and provide a valuable basis for further progress towards a climate-neutral value chain.”

An ABS warning light is on, and the scan tool shows a wheel speed sensor code. On many late-model vehicles, the sensor is part of the hub bearing assembly. That can make replacing the hub seem like the fastest solution.
But a wheel speed sensor code does not automatically condemn the sensor, bearing or hub assembly; it identifies a circuit or signal that needs to be tested.
Before replacing an expensive hub unit, confirm the integrity of the sensor, wiring and ABS module supply circuit.

Begin by verifying the complaint. Record all ABS, stability-control, communication and low-voltage codes before clearing anything. Check the code description and failure subtype in current service information. A circuit-open code, an implausible-signal code and an erratic-signal code can require different diagnostic approaches.
Next, monitor all four wheel-speed data parameters while rotating the wheels or driving the vehicle at low speed.
Compare the readings. Does one wheel remain at zero? Does its speed drop out intermittently? Does it report a different speed than the other three wheels?

This confirms which corner is producing the questionable data, but it still does not prove the hub is defective. The problem could be the sensor, magnetic encoder, connector, wiring harness, module supply voltage or even the vehicle’s electrical system.
The next step is to test the signal as close to the sensor as possible.

A 2011 Toyota Camry equipped with a U660E transmission has come into the shop in default with a trouble code U0101 “Lost Communication With TCM” set. Because the scan tool could not communicate with the TCM, this code was retrieved from other modules that normally would communicate with the TCM.
Once power and grounds to the TCM were verified to be good and no wiring issues were found, the TCM was condemned as the component causing the complaint.
A used TCM was temporarily connected and although it stored a variety of other codes, it did communicate with the scan tool.

There are several valid reasons for a shop to choose a used module to replace the failed component. In the case of Toyota, it is important to match the two 10-digit numbers on the TCM as well as the manufacturing point of origin.
The U660E/U760E TCMs are manufactured in two locations, one in Japan (see Figure 1, above left), and the other in the USA (see Figure 2, above right).
TCMs from these two locations are not interchangeable and neither are non-matching build numbers.
When replacing a failed TCM with a good used one, be sure to match both sets of ten-digit numbers as another safety measure in obtaining the correct TCM.
Modern brake systems use faster valves, tighter internal passages and more frequent automatic brake interventions than systems used 20 years ago.

As a result, many late-model vehicles require lower-viscosity brake fluid. The goal is to maintain efficient fluid movement at low temperatures so the hydraulic unit can build and release pressure quickly.

Lower-viscosity brake fluid plays a growing role in modern brake systems. Today’s vehicles require brake fluid to move quickly through hydraulic control units that support ABS, stability control, traction control and several ADAS braking functions.
Lower-Viscosity Brake Fluid Supports Faster Response
The ABS hydraulic unit is no longer used only during panic stops.
It may also apply and release brake pressure for electronic stability control, traction control, adaptive cruise control, collision mitigation braking and automatic emergency braking.

Inside the hydraulic control unit, brake fluid moves through small valves and narrow passages. Lower viscosity allows pressure to increase and decrease faster, helping the system make quicker and more precise braking corrections.
Brake fluid condition is also important. Moisture contamination can increase viscosity, lower the boiling point and raise corrosion risk.
Technicians should use the exact brake fluid specified by the vehicle manufacturer and replace it according to the proper service information.

California will elect its next insurance commissioner on Nov. 3, as incumbent Ricardo Lara is term-limited.
The insurance commissioner seat is elected for four years and is limited to serving two terms.
Sens. Ben Allen and Jane Kim, a consumer advocate and an attorney, will be on this year’s midterm ballot. Both are Democrats.
Allen has served in the state’s legislature since 2014, according to his campaign website. He lists climate and environmental policies as a focus during his tenure.
The website also lists work on strengthening transparency, including expanding ballot access and championing the DISCLOSE Act.
“He has consistently scored tops in the legislature in the California Clean Money Campaign’s reports for his commitment to transparency and political reform,” the website states.
Allen’s plan focuses on strengthening the state’s insurance market as wildfires and climate disasters intensify.

“My plan will restore a competitive insurance market, ensure Californians are treated fairly after disasters, and build resilient communities that can withstand the climate challenges ahead,” he states on his website.
Fighting insurers that “deny and delay” and post-disaster insurer compliance are other planned action items, Allen’s site claims.
This would include higher upfront payments for coverage requiring insurers to clearly explain claim denials and maintain post-disaster real-time reporting on delays and outstanding claims.
modernize customer service and filings infrastructure, improve consumer communication, and provide data transparency.

Kim previously served on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, as California political director for Bernie Sanders, and as California director for the Working Families Party, according to her campaign website.
Her priorities focus on “affordable, available insurance for all,” the website states. She proposes a single-payer disaster insurance policy for state residents.
The website also says she’ll ensure premiums cover claims, or lower them.

“Insurance companies should spend premium dollars on their intended purpose: protecting policyholders,” the website states. “If companies collect more than they need to cover claims and a reasonable profit, that money should go back to policyholders or be invested in statewide resilience, not huge payouts at our expense — like the $27 million salary one insurance company CEO was paid last year.”
Her site states that a long-term goal is to build a public auto insurance option to compete in the market.
She also notes that she’s focused on “fast and fair claims.” This includes freezing rates when a claim is filed, penalizing delays to speed up payments, and immediate payouts.

Under Kim, insurance companies would be held accountable through market conduct examinations and elevated complaint rates, according to the website. She also proposes an insurance performance dashboard that consumers can use to assess insurer risks before choosing a policy.

Oklahoma, California, and Georgia are the states where policyholders are most likely to feel influenced by a new insurance commissioner on their home insurance premiums, according to an Insurify analysis.
California saw a 5% homeowners insurance increase last year, the analysis found. It also found home insurance rates have increased 22% since 2023.

New commercial vehicle safety ratings from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) show that cargo vans and heavy-duty pickups lag behind passenger vehicles in front crash prevention.

While IIHS says marginal and poor ratings are common among the first commercial vehicles put through vehicle-to-vehicle and pedestrian crash avoidance tests, at least one performs well in each test, “showing that meeting the challenge is not out of reach for manufacturers.”

“These results are a wake-up call for commercial vehicle makers,” said IIHS President David Harkey in a press release. “Front crash prevention is especially important for these larger, heavier vans and trucks because of the danger they pose to other road users.”
Cargo vans scored the highest in both tests. The Mercedes-Benz Sprinter 2500 earned a good rating for vehicle-to-vehicle front crash prevention.
The Chevrolet BrightDrop 400 and Rivian RCV-Delivery 500 earned good ratings for pedestrian crash avoidance.
IIHS launched its commercial vehicle assessment program in June, including driver protection information.

“That part of the assessment checks for essential features such as standard front and side airbags, advanced seatbelt technology, and effective seatbelt reminders,” the IIHS press release states. “Many government standards for passenger vehicles, including airbag requirements, don’t apply to delivery vans, box trucks, tractor-trailers, and larger work pickups.

“Unlike the driver protection evaluation, the vehicle-to-vehicle front crash prevention and pedestrian front crash prevention evaluations use the Institute’s scale of good, acceptable, marginal, or poor. The test protocols and rating requirements are the same as those used for passenger vehicles.”

IIHS notes that 6,215 people were killed in crashes involving heavy- or medium-duty vehicles or light vans in 2024, accounting for 16% of all roadway fatalities in the U.S. It adds that reducing that toll is a key part of the Institute’s 30×30 vision of reducing fatalities 30% by 2030.

The initial evaluations focus on cargo vans and Class 3 pickup trucks. Class 3 pickups have a gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) of 10,001 to 14,000 pounds. GVWR is the maximum weight a vehicle can safely carry, including passengers, cargo, and the vehicle’s weight.

IIHS will continue to evaluate Class 3 vehicles this year and next, adding ratings for headlights and rear automatic emergency braking (AEB), according to the release. The Institute plans to phase in trucks in classes four through six later.

The Chevrolet Express 2500 and the GMC Savana 2500 cargo vans earn poor ratings in the vehicle-to-vehicle and pedestrian tests because they lack AEB. IIHS says AEB is an optional feature only available on vehicles with a forward collision warning system.

Performance varied widely among the other vans and pickup trucks in the vehicle-to-vehicle test. The test evaluates forward collision warning and AEB at different speeds with a passenger car target and a motorcycle target. It also evaluates forward collision warning with a semitrailer.
The Sprinter 2500 earned a good rating, the BrightDrop 400 an acceptable rating, and the others marginal or poor.
IIHS found that the motorcycle target was the biggest challenge. In most motorcycle trials, several of the systems failed to issue warnings or slow down at all.

At most speeds, others successfully slowed to avoid or mitigate collisions with the motorcycle and passenger car targets, but were downgraded because they didn’t provide timely warnings to the driver.
Overall, the vehicles performed better in the pedestrian evaluation than in the vehicle-to-vehicle test, IIHS said.
The pedestrian test represents common daytime and nighttime crashes involving an adult or child crossing the road or an adult walking in the travel lane.

Among cargo vans, the BrightDrop 400 and RCV-Delivery 500 earned good ratings, and the Sprinter 2500 earned an acceptable rating. Among Class 3 pickups, the F-350 and Ram 3500 earned acceptable ratings.
Several vehicles, including the F-350 and Ram 3500, had a harder time detecting and avoiding the child pedestrian dummy in daylight conditions than the adult at night.

“The problem may be related to the shorter height of the child dummy and the tall front ends of the vehicles,” the release states. “That’s because the sensors used for detection are positioned near the rearview mirror. In some instances, the child dummy was detected at a distance but then ‘disappeared’ as the vehicle got closer.”

The poor and marginal systems also failed to slow down enough in most of the nighttime trials with the adult. Those trials are done with low-beam headlights and then again with high beams. Others performed worse at the slowest test speed.

A recent bill introduced in the U.S. Senate promises cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth nationwide, according to the bill sponsors.

U.S. Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Mike Lee (R-UT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) on Sept. 30.

The sponsors say the BAAJA provides certainty that permitted energy and infrastructure projects will retain their permits, except under extraordinary circumstances, violations of law, a court order, or targeted reforms for energy projects.
The bill would expedite project approvals by amending the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Historic Preservation Act.

“For far too long, our broken and outdated federal environmental review and permitting processes have stood in the way of energy reliability, secure jobs, modern infrastructure, and economic growth,” said Capito in a press release about the bill. “The bipartisan reforms we secured in this deal will transform our nation’s ability to power our economy and fuel future growth, while continuing to protect the land, water, and wildlife we all cherish.”
Lee added that permitting often delays building infrastructure.

“[W]hat too often stands in the way is a permitting system that takes too long and costs too much,” he said. “After years of work in Congress and many months of negotiations, I’m proud we’ve reached a bipartisan agreement to fix this broken process and get America back to building.”

John Bozzella, president and CEO of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation (Auto Innovators), made a similar argument in support of the bill as it relates to the automotive industry, backing the bill sponsors’ plan to increase domestic production of critical manufacturing elements.

“The auto industry in America supports our economic and national security,” Bozzella wrote in a statement of support for the bill. “For the auto sector to remain competitive in today’s global marketplace, it’s essential to have reliable access to energy and the critical minerals that power our advanced vehicles.

“Sens. Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich understand this dynamic and have a plan to make American permitting more predictable by increasing domestic production of elements that are critical to the country’s largest manufacturing sector. We know that when those supply chains are disrupted, it can ripple across the country’s industrial base.”
He added that the bill is key to increasing advanced manufacturing, economic growth, jobs, and protecting the country’s defense base.

The Automotive National and Economic Security Act of 2026 was introduced in the U.S. House in August to study the national and economic security risks foreign adversaries, such as China, pose to the U.S. automotive industry, according to a press release from bill sponsor Rep. Diana Harshbarger’s (R-TN). She co-sponsors the bill with Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-MI).
- “Foreign ownership of, and state-directed investment in, U.S. automakers by foreign military organizations, political parties, and state-owned enterprises.
- “Joint ventures, subsidiaries, and commercial partnerships between U.S. manufacturers and foreign adversaries.
- “Transfers of critical and emerging technologies to foreign adversaries.
- “Impacts on U.S. national security, economic competitiveness, and intellectual property protection.”
The Bipartisan Policy Center published an explainer of the 411-page BAAJA, drilling down to how each environmental and energy act listed above would change if the bill passes.

The National Environmental Policy Act’s procedural provisions would be rewritten “along three lines: scope of review (what agencies must analyze), which projects get reviewed at all, and how long the process takes,” according to the explainer.

The Bipartisan Policy Center adds in its explainer that the BAAJA would amend the Clean Water Act to reduce friction caused by some of the provisions on linear infrastructure and industrial facilities permitting while still protecting waters.
The explainer states the BAAJA would tighten consultation and approval timelines under the Endangered Species Act “without changing the jeopardy standard or the criteria for listing a species.”
BAAJA would “write a narrower definition” into Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. Section 106 deals with funding and permit issuance for projects that affect historic properties.
“The result is that the federal approval, not the entire project footprint, would set the boundaries of review,” the explainer states.

The Bipartisan Policy Center covers several other aspects of the proposed amendments, including power sector emissions, electricity costs, grid data access, ratepayer protection from data centers, and more.
According to Whitehouse, if the BAAJA passes, the U.S. power grid will be flooded with clean, affordable energy.

“America is entering a new era of energy demand,” he said in the release. “We have an enormous opportunity to build big things again to meet that moment — to build more generation, expand our grid, create more jobs, lower energy costs, and make sure we have the energy we need to compete. It should not take decades to build the infrastructure our country needs.”

CCC Intelligent Solutions Inc. (CCC) has announced an integration with Azimuth Claims Solutions, bringing Azimuth’s ADAS calibration identification and labor time capabilities to the CCC ONE platform.

The integration connects Azimuth’s ADAS calibration recommendations to CCC ONE, enabling repair facilities to view recommendations within their existing workflow. Azimuth combines OEM procedures, vehicle build data and real-world time studies to help identify required OEM calibration operations and associated labor times.

Repairers will be able to add Azimuth recommendations to the estimate to help reduce manual steps and support more efficient, consistent repair planning. As advanced driver-assistance systems become more common, identifying calibration requirements has become a more complex and critical part of the collision repair process.
Integrating Azimuth with CCC ONE gives repairers access to actionable calibration information earlier in the repair process without requiring them to move between separate systems.

“ADAS technology continues to add complexity to the repair process, making it increasingly important for repairers to have the right information available at the right time,” said Dan Risley, vice president, market solutions, automotive services group at CCC Intelligent Solutions. “By integrating Azimuth with CCC ONE, we’re giving repairers another way to access actionable calibration recommendations within their existing workflow, helping them make informed decisions and keep repairs moving.”

Azimuth’s platform is designed to bring greater transparency and consistency to ADAS calibration planning by identifying required OEM procedures and labor associated with the vehicle and repair. The company’s technology helps insurers and collision repairers navigate increasingly complex calibration requirements as vehicle systems continue to evolve.

“ADAS calibration has become one of the most critical and least standardized components of modern collision repair,” said Charles Rich, CEO of Azimuth Claims Solutions. “With sensors, cameras and software-driven systems now involved in nearly every repair, the industry needs clearer, more consistent guidance to determine what procedures are required. By bringing Azimuth’s calibration identification engine and labor time intelligence into the CCC ONE platform, CCC is helping deliver the level of transparency, consistency and workflow support that repairers and insurers expect from a modern, data-driven ecosystem. This collaboration enables a more informed, unified view of ADAS requirements tied directly to the repair plan, supporting better outcomes as vehicles continue their evolution into software-defined platforms.”

The addition of Azimuth expands CCC’s diagnostics network and reflects the company’s focus on connecting collision repairers with the tools, information and partners they need to navigate increasingly complex vehicle technology and repair requirements.

The automotive and powersports aftermarket will recognize its innovators, leaders and visionaries during the 2026 SEMA Industry Honors on Thursday, Nov. 5 at the BleauLive Theater inside the Fontainebleau Las Vegas.

Held during the 2026 SEMA Show, SEMA Industry Honors is the industry’s annual celebration of the people whose creativity, leadership and passion continue to move the automotive and powersports aftermarket forward. The evening will recognize the SEMA Hall of Fame Class of 2026, SEMA Content Creator of the Year, SEMA Person of the Year and the recipient of the Robert E. Petersen Lifetime Achievement Award.

“SEMA Industry Honors brings our community together around the people, ideas and achievements that are shaping the future of the aftermarket,” said Tom Gattuso, vice president of events for SEMA. “By celebrating industry legends alongside today’s most influential leaders and storytellers, the event connects the aftermarket’s proud history with its next chapter. It is an opportunity for everyone at the SEMA Show to recognize excellence, strengthen relationships and be inspired by the individuals moving our industry forward.”

The program will be emceed by Kevin Oeste, who will guide attendees through an evening of recognition, personal stories and celebration. Members of the SEMA community and other familiar faces from the automotive world will also take the stage to help honor this year’s award recipients.
Celebrating the Industry’s Highest Achievements

The SEMA Hall of Fame is the association’s highest honor, recognizing individuals whose careers and contributions have helped shape and advance the automotive specialty equipment industry. The 2026 SEMA Hall of Fame class includes Doug Dwyer, Jay Leno, Ellen McKoy and Dennis Overholser.
Members of SEMA’s Councils & Networks will participate in the Hall of Fame presentations, helping recognize the inductees’ contributions and lasting impact on the industry.
SEMA Industry Honors will also recognize outstanding achievements in leadership, automotive storytelling and lifetime contributions to the specialty automotive industry.
The SEMA Person of the Year award honors an individual whose leadership, service and contributions have significantly strengthened the industry and the SEMA community.

The SEMA Content Creator of the Year award recognizes an individual who uses compelling and innovative content to expand the reach of the automotive lifestyle, engages new audiences and inspires greater participation in the industry.

Presented by the Petersen Automotive Museum, the Robert E. Petersen Lifetime Achievement Award honors individuals whose careers and contributions have made a lasting impact on motorsports, particularly drag racing. Named for the museum’s late founder, Robert E. Petersen, the award is considered one of the specialty automotive industry’s highest honors.

“Guests can expect a high-energy evening that blends meaningful recognition with the camaraderie that makes the SEMA Show so special,” said Andy Tompkins, trade show director for SEMA. “From connecting with colleagues during the reception to hearing the stories behind this year’s honorees, attendees will experience an entertaining and inspiring celebration of the people who make the automotive aftermarket extraordinary.”
The evening begins at 6 p.m. with a cocktail reception, followed by the Industry Honors awards program at 7:30 p.m. (Reception will include heavy appetizers; dinner will not be served.)

In the automotive aftermarket, growth is often associated with adding more: more products, more inventory, more suppliers and more resources. However, adding more doesn’t always lead to growth. In fact, adding more can introduce unnecessary complexity, making growth more difficult. The most successful businesses understand where they create the greatest value and have the discipline to direct resources toward those priorities.

Inventory management is one area where this can be seen. Healthy inventory turns consistently for suppliers and distributors, whereas chronically slow-moving inventory can signal that resources are not creating enough value for customers. Even inventory that isn’t moving still requires dollars to acquire, manage, store and move through the operation, and these costs can add up quickly, especially when the product isn’t generating meaningful sales.

As an important proactive action, suppliers and distributors should consistently review inventory investment and turns to help identify which products are creating value and where resources can be better focused to help drive growth.

The purchase price is easy to measure, and too often, businesses try to sell for the most and buy for the least. But greater value can come from understanding what partners need and where their challenges exist.

For distributors, there’s also value in building deeper relationships with a focused group of suppliers. During periods of supply disruption or elevated demand, manufacturers and other suppliers naturally prioritize their most important customers. These relationships create opportunities to support each other’s businesses better while establishing mutual trust and confidence.

The critical learning from this example is the importance of building relationships that are strategic rather than simply transactional. The most important question is: How can we change the way we do business to benefit both sides beyond the purchase order’s value? When distributors and suppliers understand each other’s businesses well enough to answer this question, the relationship can become stronger and create better economics for both sides.

Simplification also extends to how distributors serve their customers. By providing more flexibility in terms of how customers purchase and receive products, distributors can help customers manage their inventory more efficiently while maximizing their dollars and warehouse space.

That same principle can extend across the broader supplier relationship. When customers can access more of what they need in smaller quantities and combine categories into fewer shipments, they can simplify ordering and receiving, turn inventory faster and manage working capital and space more effectively.

For Highline Warren, we start with a simple question: What do we want to be known for? We want customers to know that they can rely on us to deliver products on time and in full. Consistently delivering on those priorities builds credibility and can make a supplier more integral to the customer’s process, turning focus into a foundation for growth.

Understanding where a business creates value can also help identify its next growth opportunity. For suppliers and distributors, one of the easiest, fastest and most economical ways to grow is to sell existing products to existing customers. The relationship is already established, the supplier understands the customer, and the customer already knows the value the supplier provides. From there, a business should look at the broader market and consider how products or categories it already carries can help address another need.

For example, a retailer may buy several product categories from one supplier while sourcing other products elsewhere, even though the same supplier already carries those products. The overlap creates an opportunity to grow by leveraging existing products and capabilities.

Growth frequently happens in concentric circles: first by strengthening existing relationships, then by expanding into adjacent opportunities that align with proven capabilities. Businesses that consistently deliver value earn the right to broaden those relationships over time.

Growth isn’t always about adding more; often, it comes from getting more from the products, capabilities and relationships a business has already established. Businesses disciplined enough to focus on this approach are better positioned to support customer needs, further strengthen relationships and create opportunities for mutual success.

Oct. 24 (UPI) -- Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat in the Bavarian Alps was gutted by fire, and one man has been arrested.

The Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest, caught fire Friday night, setting off alarms at 9:25 p.m. local time in nearby Traunstein. Firefighters arrived to find the building engulfed in flames.

Fire trucks had some difficulty getting access to the site "due to the local conditions," authorities said. The building is about 6,000 feet up in the Kehlstein mountain, and visitors had to access it via a long tunnel leading to an elevator that travels up about 40 stories. Only specially designed buses have regular access to the road to the tunnel.
The fire was still burning early Saturday, police said, with about 200 emergency personnel on the scene. No injuries were reported.
Police said Saturday that the building wasn't likely salvageable. They also offered no details about the person arrested, saying the investigation was ongoing.

The building was completed in 1938 and was a guesthouse for Nazi officials and their visitors. Hitler also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films showing him as a lover of animals and nature.
It became a tourist attraction in the 1950s, and until Friday offered Alpine views and a restaurant. The Kehlstein mountain is a subpeak of the Hoher Gӧll, which overlooks the town of Berchtesgaten.

Farther down the mountain is the Obersalzburg Documentation Center, which tells the story of the building and Nazi use of the site and offers entrance to some of the mountain tunnels where Nazis hid during the war.
The Kehlsteinhaus and the mountain tunnels and bunkers were graffitied by Allied soldiers who liberated the area.

Iran has increased efforts to target U.S. personnel in the Middle East and other countries, according to a memo sent by the Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday.

LONDON — Police in the British capital said Saturday that they received a letter containing allegations about the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019, but did not tell other law enforcement agencies.
Authorities in the Philippines confirmed this week that they are investigating Thomas Markle over claims that he kept child sexual abuse images at his home. He has denied the allegations.

The elder Markle, 82, denied the reported allegations, calling them “sick lies” in a statement to Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper. He added they were “the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

PARIS — More than 100,000 people marched in Paris on Saturday over school funding and soaring living costs, challenging President Emmanuel Macron’s government as police fired tear gas and water cannons near the end of the protest.
Paris police estimated turnout at 110,000, with demonstrators mobilizing despite restrictions that confined the march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the center.

Police used tear gas in several cities, including Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, and Strasbourg, and water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported. In Marseille, officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march’s endpoint.

The Paris prosecutor’s office said 64 people had been arrested in connection with Saturday’s demonstration and 40 placed in police custody. Those arrested included six minors. Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said.

The unrest is testing Macron’s authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May. The stakes are high: the far-right National Rally has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes for them.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had announced a nationwide deployment of up to 70,000 officers, backed by helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.

Authorities had confined the Paris march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the center. An Associated Press journalist saw tens of thousands of people marching from Porte d’Italie early in the afternoon. Trade unions led the procession, followed by protesters in raincoats carrying flags and handmade placards.
After reaching the authorized endpoint at Porte de Vincennes, some demonstrators tried to continue toward Place de la Nation, but police blocked their path, French media reported.
Camille Chesnier, 27, said she had been unable to find work despite having an engineering degree and a master’s degree.
“There are enormous numbers of people in the same situation as me but who aren’t privileged and who find themselves living on the streets and in squats and, frankly, it’s very tough,” she said.
A small protest became a national movement

What began last month as a protest over staff shortages at one high school southeast of Paris has grown into a national movement. Students demanding better schools and workers seeking higher wages and pensions have brought anger over living standards into the final months of President Emmanuel Macron’s presidency.
Energy prices in France were 21.3% higher in September than a year earlier, helping drive overall inflation to 3.1%, according to the national statistics agency, INSEE.
Macron met high school representatives Friday. They said he had promised to overhaul university admissions, but called for protests to continue until concrete measures are announced.
Police changed the Paris route Friday. At Bastille, the original starting point, police used a megaphone to tell people to leave or face a 135-euro ($150) fine.
Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, said she had been joining protests for more than 30 years but had never seen a march start at Porte d’Italie.
“They are using what happened last week as an excuse to quiet protesters,” she said. “But it won’t stop the movement. It won’t stop students from demanding better conditions in schools.”

In Marseille, police put attendance at 17,000, while the CGT union estimated 100,000. In the southwestern city of Toulouse, 26,500 people joined the protests, according to authorities. Authorities had banned rallies in cities including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier.
Trade unions have criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
Thousands also marched Saturday in Orléans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as Marine Le Pen’s National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.

Macron, a centrist, has entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.
Nuñez acknowledged Monday that police had lost control in some cities during last weekend’s unrest. He offered to resign, but Macron refused the offer.
More than half a million people took to the streets last Saturday. Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted over the weekend.

Gendarmes stood guard beneath the Arc de Triomphe as shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris. Near the Saint-Lazare train station Saturday, Akram Ahmed, a 34-year-old contractor, was boarding up an optician’s shop.
“I got the call last night,” he said. “The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life.”
Major museums, including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — were shuttered Saturday.
Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.
Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system.
Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.

Public middle and high schools lost 15.4 million teaching hours in the 2024-25 school year because absent teachers were not replaced, according to Education Ministry figures. That amounted to 7.5% of scheduled teaching time.
They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.
“The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people,” said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University.
Premier Roger Cook has visited South Hedland for the first time since an inquest into the deaths of three local children was announced.
He was met by residents angered by reports of child protection failings.
The state government says there has been progress, while community elders urge more collaboration.

South Hedland residents have confronted the West Australian Premier during a five-hour visit to the northern town — his first since the state government announced a coronial inquest into the deaths of three local children.

The renewed investigation into Margaret Hawke's 2022 killing of her 10-year-old daughter, seven-year-old son and four-month-old baby came after sustained political and media pressure over failures by WA's Department of Child Protection.

Recent weeks have seen a steady stream of political drop-ins to South Hedland, more than 1,600 kilometres north of Perth, with the premier arriving on Saturday to declare a contractor had been selected to construct a long-promised $22 million MRI facility.
However, the spotlight remained on reports first appearing in The Australian newspaper that up to 15 children had been living unsupervised in a state-owned home until September.

The Premier was accompanied by Child Protection Minister Jessica Stojkovski — her fourth trip to South Hedland in nine weeks — for an agenda dominated by closed-door discussions with government agencies and their partners.

"You've gotta come back sit with us here, camp with us and roam the streets with us, so they can see for themselves what's actually happening," said Nyamal-Pitjikarli elder Doris Eaton, who spoke with the pair at a snap meeting during their visit.
"You can't see it from Perth, you can't do fly in and fly out."
Departing talks with community organisation Hedland Aboriginal Strong Leaders, Mr Cook and Ms Stojkovski came under fire from a community member who identified herself as a former foster carer.
"When is the department going to be accountable and when are you going to speak to the community?" she said.
The ABC spoke with multiple other residents who expressed their frustration with the government response.
"I get confronted by people all the time. That's part of the job," Mr Cook said.
"But I fully appreciate that everyone wants to see things improve."
There were no policy announcements about child protection during the premier's visit, nor did he meet with families impacted by the crisis.
Mr Cook said the emphasis was on consulting with the people "who are delivering the services in the community".
The ABC understands Dorothy Papertalk, mother of Margaret Hawke and the children's grandmother, declined an invitation to meet with the premier.
Ms Papertalk led the campaign for an inquest, which was denied by the coroner in 2025. Ms Papertalk has requested privacy at this time.
"There are a range of families that are receiving good services, there's others that we can improve," Mr Cook said.
"The department's in a process of continuous improvement all the time."

When questioned, Ms Stojkovski could not point to how many full-time equivalent staff positions had been filled since it was revealed in WA Parliament the Pilbara region had 11 child protection caseworker vacancies.
A relief team has been sent to South Hedland in response.
"Having those senior staff from the group, the relieving team, is really important and it's been very helpful for our staff here on the ground," Ms Stojkovski said.
The minister expects to be handed an assurance review of recommendations made in the wake of the Hawke murders by the end of the month.
On Thursday, WA Commissioner for Children and Young People Jacqueline McGowan-Jones tabled a scathing assessment of the state's child protection system in parliament.
The report considered the experiences of 19 children who were placed into a secure care centre multiple times and made 56 recommendations.
"If children are brought into out-of-home care, it is because they are apparently at risk at home," Ms McGowan-Jones told the ABC.
"They were equally, if not more so, at risk, being brought into the state system."
WA opposition leader Basil Zempilas said it was "insulting" that the premier was not visiting affected families.
"I am absolutely astounded after nine weeks of this being in the national spotlight, the premier has finally gone up — finally — but is not meeting with any families," he said.
"This is a shocking and ignorant lack of leadership."

Why a new round in the U.S.-Iran conflict could be the most devastating yet
Domestic politics appear poised to trigger a new phase of war with Iran
The warning signs are flashing red with indications that once the ballots are counted in the U.S. midterm elections, the United States and Israel will relaunch their war with Iran.
The next round of attacks could be more devastating than the first, warn analysts.

"A renewed war seems almost inevitable," said Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli Middle East and Iran analyst whose earlier warnings and cautions about the risks of a direct conflict with Iran were largely borne out by events.

Citrinowicz, who worked for Israel's military as an intelligence official for more than two decades, had initially warned that any U.S. and Israeli attack on the Islamic regime would not likely lead to regime change but would instead end up engulfing the entire region in a wider conflict — an assessment that proved true.
In an interview with CBC News, he said that assessment still holds.
"The problem is there is no silver bullet solution to the impasse we are now at in the Persian Gulf and in front of Trump he has only bad and worse options."

Under U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, their countries broke with decades of restraint and shadow warfare and launched two distinct wars with Iran over the past 18 months.
Iranian women look at a building, which was damaged in a U.S. and Israeli strike in March, in Tehran on Aug. 22. (Reuters)
The first in June 2025 began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, lasted 12 days and ended with a fragile ceasefire.

The conflict roared back to life in February of this year following a massive U.S. military buildup in the region. It began with Israel's strikes against Iran's senior leadership, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Citrinowicz, who's with Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, said a third round of war could be the worst yet, based on what Iranian officials are telegraphing.

"They will attack the energy facilities in the Gulf. But more than that, they will cause significant damage to civilian infrastructure, communications, as well as cutting off the internet lines going under [the] Hormuz Strait," he said.
He said there is even a possibility that Iran could push some of its massive land army into the fight with limited assaults against Gulf countries that house U.S. bases, such as Kuwait and Bahrain.
"We'll see a regional war with Iran investing a lot in attacking the U.S. presence in the region to cause maximum economical damage to the U.S. international economy."

Smoke rises from a burning vessel, following what the U.S. Central Command said was a strike on an Iranian-affiliated dhow, at a location given as the Gulf of Oman, in this still image taken from a video released on Oct. 14. (U.S. Central Command/Reuters)

While both sides have largely avoided fresh strikes against each other's bases or territory since the summer truce collapsed, the conflict remains active. The U.S. imposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports and Iran has continued to target commercial shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, driving up global energy costs.

Posting on Truth Social Thursday, Trump blamed Iran for trying to artificially drive up oil prices ahead of the midterms on Nov. 3, elections that many pollsters believe will see Trump's Republicans lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate as well.
"They are even making up fake hits, mines and everything else," said Trump, implying that Iran is exaggerating the extent of the damage it's causing.

A report published this week by the Washington, D.C.,-based Critical Threats Project alongside the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) also suggested Iran is trying to use strikes on shipping to weaken Trump's position heading into the elections.

"The increase in Iranian attacks on vessels is part of the ongoing Iranian campaign to pressure the United States to meet Iranian demands, including control over the Strait, by driving up global prices," the report said.
People walk on the beach, with vessels in the Strait of Hormuz visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Oct. 13. (Razieh Poudat West Asia News Agency/Reuters)

Iran's government wants relief from punishing sanctions, reparations for the damage caused by earlier U.S.-Israel strikes, the release of billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets and the right to keep its supplies of enriched uranium.
Mediators with Pakistan and Qatar have spent weeks trying to push diplomatic solutions to get the two sides talking again, but to no avail.
For both Netanyahu and Trump, the war with Iran remains unfinished business.

The Islamic regime not only remains in power, but its leadership has also proven remarkably adept at adapting to both the military strikes and the economic blockade imposed by the West.

"The war in some respects has probably persuaded Iran's leadership to double down on their commitment to the revolutionary ideology that has really forged this regime," said Suzanne Maloney, a vice-president and director of the foreign policy program at the Washington, D.C.,-based Brookings Institution.
Like Citroniwicz, she said if war resumes, Trump won't be able to easily contain it.
"The retaliation as we've seen will come not just from Iran, but from its proxies and partners in the region," she said, referring to the Houthi militias in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
Iran's goal won't just be to hit back at U.S. military targets but also soft economic targets, such as airports, that could undermine Gulf countries for years to come, she said.
Maloney and Karim Sadjadpour, a prominent Iran expert with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, were speaking on an online Carnegie panel about the future of the war in Iran.
"I genuinely don't think that President Trump has a clear idea in his head what he's trying to achieve," said Sadjadpour.
"I don't see any possibility of what Trump is looking for — which is like a knockout punch, a military strike — which will essentially force the Iranians into a compromise or capitulation."
Trump claimed his justification for the initial attacks on Iran was to ensure the country doesn't get a nuclear weapon.

At the time, while Iran possessed enough enriched uranium to theoretically pursue a weapon, many independent experts and U.S. intelligence sources believed it was still likely months away from doing so — and perhaps more importantly, that the regime's supreme leader had not yet made the definitive political decision to cross the nuclear threshold.
Since those initial June 2025 strikes, the human cost of the war has been severe.
Western NGOs claim the death toll in Iran is well over 7,000, including civilians and government figures who have been killed in the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes.
Lebanon has also suffered an especially heavy toll, with local media reporting more than 4,000 fatalities.
Twenty-one U.S. service members were killed, mostly by Iranian strikes on U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf, while more than 70 Israelis have died.
People drive near a billboard depicting U.S. President Donald Trump on a building in Tehran on Sept. 16. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA/Reuters)
There have also been deaths throughout the Gulf countries, including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, as well as in Iraq and Yemen.
The New York Times and other U.S. media are reporting the Pentagon is working on a new battle plan for the possible next round of attacks — but whether Trump will ultimately authorize it is unknown.
Israel's leadership, on the other hand, has made no secret of its push to restart the conflict, with Netanyahu explicitly stating his desire to bring down the Iran regime by "finishing the job."
Netanyahu faces Israeli voters in the coming days, and whether he hangs onto his job could end up in a photo finish.

Relaunching the war with Iran could offer him a tactical way to stay in power; even if his party loses seats, a widening security crisis could lead to the creation of an emergency unity government with members of the opposition, said Citrinowicz.

"The real risk is that Netanyahu will involve his political considerations together with some other operational development in Iran that he is going to not necessarily invent, but probably [inflate]," he said.
A shopkeeper works at his shop in a local market in Tehran on Sept. 26. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency/Reuters)
"And this combination will lead to an unnecessary attack against Iran."
Sadjadpour from the Carnegie panel said there is no obvious military way out of the impasse and says Trump's maximalist goals have closed down diplomatic options as well.

"I believe there's a pretty clear formula under which it [Iran's government] compromises," said Sadjadpour. "It's when it faces what I would describe as existential economic pressure, coupled with a clear, limited diplomatic exit.
"If you're asking them to change their identity, that's not going to succeed."
Israelis are leaving the country in record numbers. Could a looming election accelerate the trend?
A February study found 99,000 Israelis left the country in 2023 and 2024
Sitting at his desk in a sun-filled apartment in Tel Aviv, economist Itai Ater pored over data that shows more Israelis have left the country over the past three years than ever before.

Those have been tumultuous years for the country of around 10 million people, with war, economic uncertainty and a prime minister plagued by corruption charges whose trial started in 2020 and still hasn't reached a verdict.

Ater, a professor at the Coller School of Management at Tel Aviv University, says these departures could accelerate depending on the outcome of next week's legislative elections, destabilizing the country's economy and causing ripple effects throughout the region.

"Israelis are thinking, 'do I want to raise my kids in a country like this?'" Ater said. "Unfortunately, and I understand, I sympathize with their answers, many of them realize that the answer is no. And that's why they're leaving."

In February, Ater and his colleagues published a study using data collected from the Central Bureau of Statistics that found 99,000 Israelis left the country between January 2023 and December 2024. The study looked at Israelis who left for at least three consecutive months and stayed out of the country for more than 270 days during the first year of their departure.
Ater says he understands why people might want to leave: 'Israelis are thinking, "do I want to raise my kids in a country like this?"' (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)

According to the data, 50,000 left in 2023, a year that saw Hamas militants storm southern Israel, killing roughly 1,200 people and kidnapping another 250. Israel responded by embarking on a devastating military campaign in the Gaza Strip that continued until a fragile ceasefire went into effect in October 2025, though Israel still controls roughly 60 per cent of the enclave and engages in regular military activity there.
In 2024, 49,000 left. Ater says preliminary data shows the trend continued in 2025, and he believes the looming election could push those numbers even higher in 2026.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has been a defining figure in Israeli politics for the past three decades and is by far the country's longest serving leader, is once again vying for power.

Polls suggest his far-right bloc will fall short of the requisite 61 seats in the Knesset to form a government and that a rival bloc headed by Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, is currently in position to secure the most seats. As of now, Eisenkot's coalition is expected to be short of a majority.
- Analysis Netanyahu's future uncertain as Israel starts to prepare for national election

Israel's multiparty system, in which coalitions are often required in order to form a government, means the election results are often only just the beginning of the intrigue and lead to a jostling of parties and power in the days after the vote.
Netanyahu has long been considered a master at this process.

A supporter of Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the Likud party, displays a flag depicting him at Mahane Yehuda market, ahead of Israel's national election, in Jerusalem on Oct. 22. (Kevin Coombs/Reuters)

"We are really, really, really terrified in the sense that if there is no change in the patterns, then there's no change in October in the elections," Ater said. "These [emigration] numbers will go up dramatically."
Avigail Ben-Porat, 50, said she dreams of leaving but doesn't have the resources to do so.
The single mother lives in Kiryat Shmona, near the Israel-Lebanon border, where she said she still regularly hears the sound of rocket fire.

"I would go and never look back," Ben-Porat said. "Most of my friends are living abroad, some of them in Portugal, some of them moved to Canada. Some of them are in Thailand and in Goa in India. They pretty much left and fled."
It's not just the volume of people leaving that has Ater and others concerned — it's their jobs.

Ater's study suggests that 2023 and 2024 saw a dramatic increase in the number of doctors, Ph.D. holders and engineers leaving the country, with 2,360 net departures from Israeli engineers and 509 net departures from doctors.
"Israel's economy depends on the human capital," he said. "It's the tech industry, it's academia, it's health care. We need these best individuals to stay in Israel."
Lawyer Liam Schwartz, seen in Tel Aviv in September, says many companies, under pressure from investors, are moving chunks of their business outside Israel. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)
Liam Schwartz oversees the corporate immigration department at Goldfarb, Gross, Seligman, an Israeli law firm based in Tel Aviv. He said Israeli companies are also eying the exit.

"There are a good deal of Israeli companies that are just — they call it business viability," Schwartz said. "They have to answer to their shareholders who are not necessarily Israeli and investors who are not necessarily Israeli and they are concerned about the viability of business operations based in Israel. So they are more willing to move chunks of their workforce to North America or to Europe."
Schwartz believes the discontent started when the government proposed judicial reforms that would have stripped power away from the Supreme Court back in January 2023.

France deploys thousands of police amid a new wave of protests
Major museums, including the Louvre and Grand Palais, closed Saturday over protest-related concerns

Paris braced for a fresh march by students and workers over school funding and soaring living costs Saturday, one week after unrest left shops looted and cars burned. The new march was restricted to the city's southeastern edge as police deployed in force across France.

Scenes of looting, burned-out cars and attacks on public buildings left the impression that the government had lost control, as groups of masked vandals targeted businesses in Paris and other city centres.
Police imposed the new route Friday between Porte d'Italie and Porte de Vincennes, replacing the planned march from Bastille to Nation.

The movement began last month over staff shortages at one high school southeast of Paris. It now reaches well beyond the classroom. Students want more teachers, better school buildings and more university places. Unions are demanding higher wages and pensions to help people meet the cost of living.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons. In central Paris, a few dozen gendarmes, or military police officers, were stationed beneath the Arc de Triomphe and along the nearby avenues.
A massive turnout is expected again after more than half a million took to the streets last week.
Museums are closed and shopkeepers are worried

Major museums, including the Louvre, Musée d'Orsay, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — are closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.

Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near the Saint-Lazare train station, Akram Ahmed, a 34-year-old contractor, was boarding up an optician's shop.
"I got the call last night," he said. "The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life."

Following the unrest, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure urged Parisian shopkeepers to hire security guards. He later clarified that protecting business owners and their establishments is the responsibility of the government.
Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend.

Protest marches are scheduled in Paris and Marseille, but some other rallies, including in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, have been banned by local authorities. In Lyon, French media reported that police used tear gas Saturday morning.

Cities outside Paris were hit hard by the unrest. Two suspects in the fire that nearly destroyed Limoges's 19th-century city hall were placed under formal investigation and held pending trial, French media reported. The probe includes attempted murder of a public official.

French President Emmanuel Macron, a centrist, has entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term, with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings.
French police move people away to prevent gatherings at the Place de la Bastille in Paris as part of nationwide protests that are taking place again on Saturday. (Dylan Martinez/Reuters)

Thousands of people gathered Saturday morning for an anti-far-right protest in the city of Orléans, about 110 kilometres south of Paris. It was organized on the sidelines of a two-day congress of Marine Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring's presidential election.

Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system. Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.
They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros (around $313 Cdn) a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.

The recent death of an iconic male elephant in Sri Lanka has raised concerns over ongoing contact between humans and the giant animals, whose habitats have been greatly reduced.

The elephant known as "Kavantissa" had been considered to be the tallest living male elephant in the Sri Lanka. Thought to be around 45 years old and measuring roughly 3.3 meters tall (11 feet), he roamed Sri Lanka's northwest near the village of Galgamuwa, and was widely admired for his majestic stature.

In late September, villagers noticed the 5.5 ton-tusker (5,500 kg) was limping, and a closer look reveled a gunshot wound on his right leg. Despite the intervention of veterinary surgeons, the elephant died on October 16.

Sri Lanka records the highest number of elephant deaths annually and the second highest number of human deaths globally from violent interactions between elephants and humans, which usually happen when crop raiding elephants encroach on farmlands.
According to official statistics, since 2019, an average of 370 elephants and 125 humans have died in human-elephant conflict incidents each year.
The situation affects the natural habitats of elephants and the livelihoods of rural communities.
Home to about 10% of the global Asian elephant population and occupying about 2% of their total natural range, Sri Lanka has the highest density of Asian elephants in the world.

The Sri Lankan elephant is an endangered subspecies in the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species, and protected under Sri Lankan law, with punishment by fines and jail terms for wildlife-related offences.
During the past few decades, forest cover in Sri Lanka has shrunk as the population has grown.
Statistics show the rural population of Sri Lanka increased from 8.25 million in 1960 to 17.8 million in 2020.
Agriculture remains the primary source of income for these rural communities. As a result, the land is cleared for agricultural activities.

According to Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC) statistics, in 2024, an estimated 7,451 wild elephants were recorded in Sri Lanka. About 70% of these wild elephants live outside protected areas.
Research shows elephants have a massive daily dietary requirement of about 150 kilograms (330 lbs.) of green matter, which drives them into farmland.

"Driven primarily by habitat loss, agricultural expansion, fragmentation of elephant corridors, and increasing competition for land and resources, human-elephant conflict continues to cause hundreds of elephant deaths and more than 100 human fatalities annually," said Ravi Corea, President of Sri Lanka Wildlife Conservation Society, a Sri Lankan non-profit conservation organization.
The conservationist told DW that rural communities are severely affected, and the agricultural losses caused by elephants can threaten a family's primary source of food and income.

"This distinguishes human-elephant conflict from many human-wildlife conflicts in economically developed countries, where wildlife encounters, although sometimes serious, generally do not threaten household subsistence to the same extent," he said.
"Despite the efforts by the government to mitigate HEC, the numbers are rising demonstrating the continuing severity of the crisis," Corea added.
Elephants are shot, poisoned, or killed by improvised explosives hidden in food and train collisions, experts say.
In view of the escalation of human-elephant conflict, the Sri Lankan government in 2020 drafted a national action plan to mitigate the problem.

"The 2020 Action Plan provides a valuable foundation for reducing human–elephant conflict, but its recommendations must be strengthened through a comprehensive national conservation strategy with enforceable habitat protection at its core," Corea said.

"The ultimate measure of success must be not merely a reduction in human–elephant conflict, but the permanent protection of ecologically connected habitats, the survival of viable wild elephant populations and the ability of people and elephants to coexist sustainably for generations to come," he added.
Community-level initiatives protect people and elephants

Meanwhile, community-based programs by non-government organizations have proven effective and sustainable. These initiatives are complemented by elephant monitoring, scientific research, habitat assessments, community education, and the development of locally appropriate deterrents, Corea said

"Our flagship initiative Project Orange Elephant in Sri Lanka's Wasgamuwa region promotes the cultivation of citrus which elephants do not like to eat as a trophic deterrence. This reduces crop raiding while generating alternative income for farmers," Corea added, pointing to things like electric fencing protecting settlements and agricultural lands while encouraging local responsibility.
Another issue is confrontations on elephant corridors, that in some cases have discouraged children from walking to school.
Elephant corridors are designated strips of land that connect larger forest and habitat patches, allowing elephants to move safely between them for food, water, breeding, and seasonal migration.

To address this, the "EleFriendly" bus service in Wasgamuwa, provides safe transportation for schoolchildren through elephant corridors and has reduced dangerous human-elephant encounters along its original route by over 90%.
"An ethically just solution must protect human lives, livelihoods, and elephant populations simultaneously, said Kamal Shashendra, a Sri Lanka-based environmental ethics researcher.

He told DW that this required scientifically informed land-use planning, protection of elephant corridors, appropriate community-based fencing, effective early-warning systems, and fair compensation for affected families.
On Tuesday, the parliament of Libya unanimously approved a maritime agreement with Turkey to establish a direct maritime economic corridor between the countries.

Turkey had agreed on the corridor with the UN-recognized Government of National Accord in western Libya in 2019. However, the agreement faced opposition from the rival Libyan government in the country's east. Now, though, the eastern parliament has reversed its previous opposition.
The decision, which was welcomed by Turkey's Foreign Ministry, is likely to contribute to tensions with other countries in the eastern Mediterranean — especially Greece .

The agreement establishes a direct maritime corridor between the southern coast of Turkey and the northern coast of Libya. Large oil and gas deposits have recently been discovered in the region in question — estimates suggest that natural gas reserves worth several hundred billion US dollars may lie beneath the seabed. Turkey and Libya aim to secure their economic rights to these raw materials and are seeking to jointly exploit the resources.

The planned corridor disregards Greek islands such as Crete, Karpathos and Rhodes. Greece's government insists that it possesses a comprehensive exclusive economic zone, or EEZ, around these islands and has already announced its opposition to the accord.

In a post on X, the Foreign Ministry announced that Greece firmly rejects the agreement and has the support of the European Union in doing so. "The European Union has described the Turkish-Libyan memorandum as null and void, stressing that it violates the sovereign rights of third states and is not consistent with the Law of the Sea," the ministry posted.

Similar wording came straight from Brussels. "I raised yesterday's Libyan vote on a maritime MoU with Türkiye and stressed that it infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states," Kaja Kallas, the European Union high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, posted on X.

Whose claims are legitimate in the eastern Mediterranean is the central point of contention. Greece primarily cites the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS. According to Article 121 of the convention, inhabited islands that "support an economic life of their own” have the same rights to an EEZ as the mainland. This applies to Crete, Rhodes and Lesbos.

Athens cites precedents such as a 2022 ruling by the International Court of Justicethat found that Colombia had violated the sovereign rights of Nicaragua by authorizing fishing activities in the Central American country's EEZ. The ICJ found that when interests overlap a fair demarcation must be reached that takes coastlines, geographical conditions and the implications of a potential boundary into account.

Turkey's government argues that the geography of the Mediterranean plays a special role: If every small Greek island off the coast of Turkey and Cyprus were granted a full EEZ, Turkey would be largely cut off from access to the open sea. This, the government argues, must be given greater consideration when demarcating the boundary.

Unlike Greece, Turkey has never signed UNCLOS. Therefore, it does not agree to have the dispute heard by a UN arbitration tribunal. Moreover, even international experts on the law of the sea disagree on what a "fair division” might look like in this specific case.

When Turkey pushed for the agreement in 2019, a brutal civil war was still raging in Libya. At that time, Turkey intervened militarily in the west to support the government in Tripoli, thereby repelling the offensive by eastern Libyan General Khalifa Hifter.

Since then, the relationship has changed fundamentally: A successful charm offensive by Turkey's government appears to have led to a political rapprochement with Hifter and his camp. Turkey's government now maintains mutually advantageous relations with both parts of Libya. In addition to the countries' plan to develop energy resources in the Mediterranean together, Turkish construction companies have secured contracts worth billions in recent years for Libya's reconstruction. Furthermore, the Turkish state-owned oil company TPAO and the Libyan National Oil Corporation are already working on joint plans for seismic surveys off of Libya's coast.

Turkey's government has established itself as a new military partner for Hifter's forces, supplying weapons and offering training programs. In doing so, Turkey is pushing back against the influence of Egypt and Russia in eastern Libya and strengthening its role as a geopolitical player in the region.

With the agreement now approved in the regional parliament, eastern Libya also aims to secure its share of the lucrative natural resources. This could give Hifter greater international influence in the future. Disputes in the eastern Mediterranean are likely to escalate further as a result of the agreement — particularly once Turkey and Libya begin extracting oil and gas from the disputed maritime area.

The agreement also jeopardizes a major project that is still in the planning stages: the EastMed pipeline, which is intended to transport natural gas from Israel and Cyprus via Greece, thereby making an important contribution to energy security in the European Union. However, the corridor established by Turkey and Libya cuts across the planned route of the pipeline. Turkey has also argued that projects involving cables or pipelines on its claimed continental shelf require its consent.

In the long term, this could lead to a division of the eastern Mediterranean region into two competing energy and defense blocs: The Turkey-Libya axis might be countered by an EU-supported alliance of Greece, Cyprus, Egypt and Israel.

Milan, Italy – Protests have been called in eight Italian cities on Saturday to demonstrate against Giorgia Meloni’s right-wing government and the rising cost of living, a week after demonstrations in Milan spiralled into clashes with police and looting.

It follows the announcement online of a new round of protests by a newly formed group calling itself the ‘October 17 Movement’, which has been the main driver of demonstrations alongside student federations, grassroots trade unions, and antiwar coalitions.
“Those who deny our future are truly violent,” it said on Instagram. “We distrust this government because we see it as authoritarian.”
In response to last weekend’s looting, the government announced a series of new security measures, including the deployment of 500 soldiers to Italy’s financial hub.

On Friday, police carried out raids and searches in several cities, against people suspected of taking part in looting and rioting in last weekend’s protests, the Italian news agency Adnkronos reported. Officers conducted another 150 raids on Saturday morning in the northern region of Lombardy.
But on its Telegram channel, the October 17 Movement said many of those planning to demonstrate wanted to voice their dissent peacefully.
“We must be peaceful. If we give [the police] an excuse, they will charge against us,” a participant identified as E said on Thursday.
Others have stressed that there is no distinction between those who engage in violence and peaceful protesters. “It’s just us,” said a member identified as Q.
Protesters decided to keep the location of the demonstration secret until the last minute. Three meeting points were expected to be announced on their social media accounts on Saturday afternoon.

In the meantime, police confirmed to Al Jazeera that they had located and were questioning the administrator of the group’s Instagram page. According to the Italian daily Corriere della Sera, he is a 30-year-old Italian-Moroccan freelance journalist and researcher. He is currently under investigation on suspicion of “inciting crimes”.
Most of the protesters arrested on Sunday were very young. Of the 271 people arrested, 220 were under the age of 18.
Some joined the protests after being unexpectedly added to a Telegram group, Corriere della Sera reported.

Lawyer Michele D’Agostino is defending two demonstrators, aged 21 and 15.

The public prosecutor has blamed social media for misleading young people into taking part in what he described as “insurrectional acts”.
Meanwhile, Justice Minister Carlo Nordio told Sky TG24 that there was a need to “expand the capacity of our youth detention facilities” in response to the mass arrests of people under the age of 18.

Earlier this week, truck drivers set up roadblocks in several regions of southern Italy to protest soaring fuel prices, leaving many markets without supplies for days. On Thursday, the government sought to offer them some relief by granting tax breaks and establishing a special fund for farmers and fishermen.

A group of gunmen stormed a Christian church in Jordan during a funeral on Friday, killing nine people and injuring more than two dozen, according to authorities.
