Police have arrested a 33-year-old German citizen after a fire ripped through Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat in Bavaria, leaving the historic Nazi meeting place – known as the Eagle’s Nest – largely destroyed.

About 200 firefighters were deployed on Friday night to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote, purpose-built Kehlsteinhaus residence, a protected building on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany.
Flames rose high into the air as firefighters approached the scene to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said, adding that nobody was injured in the fire.
Lisa Maier, a police spokesperson, said firefighters struggled to tackle the blaze due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft).
The building, which was one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era, was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said.
Built by the Nazis and formally inaugurated by Hitler on his birthday in 1939, the Eagle’s Nest has been preserved as a monument to “the insanity of the regime”, according to its website.

The building is only accessible via a road cut into the mountain through previously impassable terrain. Nazis would enter a tunnel and take a 124-metre brass lift buried in the mountain to get inside the building.

Authorities were alerted to the fire when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.15pm, police said. When firefighters arrived on the scene at about 9.50pm, the entire building was engulfed in flames.
Fire departments from six municipalities sent emergency personnel to tackle the blaze and the Bavarian Red Cross, the local mountain rescue service and the police also attended.
No reason for the fire was given, but German media reported that investigators suspected it was the result of arson. Firefighters found no one inside the building.
Efforts to fight the fire were hampered by a strong wind and rain, which turned into the year’s first snow, and firefighters had to pull out overnight after several hours.
The blaze was reportedly still burning at 7am on Saturday but appeared to be out later in the morning, although smoke continued to rise from the building.

A police spokesperson told the German tabloid Bild: “It is damaged to a large extent. The house is unlikely to be saved.” Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an Agence France-Presse photographer.
Maier said police were still investigating and would hold a news conference later on Saturday.

The 33-year-old suspect arrested by the police was a German citizen who had ties to the area but did not live there. Prosecutors said he showed signs of mental illness and after being questioned he was being sent to a psychiatric facility.
The possibility of a political motive for the blaze would be investigated, but police said there was nothing to indicate anyone else was involved.

The Eagle’s Nest was constructed between 1937 and 1938 and forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and communists in the Holocaust.
It became legendary in the postwar period and was often depicted as an essential meeting place in US war films, although in reality Hitler rarely visited the complex.
Since 1952 the building has housed an exhibition by the Institute for Contemporary History recounting its Nazi history, and a restaurant.
Officials indicated that the building, which is owned by Bavaria’s state government, would be restored after discussions with local officials, historians and conservators.
“We’re not going to leave a ruin there,” Joachim Herrmann, Bavaria’s interior minister, told reporters, adding that it was important to continue to do “the work of remembrance”.
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

In Lyon, police used teargas early on in the banned demonstration to disperse some of the crowd but people were still able to walk on.

In the last half hour there’s also a been of bit of rough activity in Marseille between police and a few dozen people. The French broadcaster BFMTV has shown live footage of masked attendees throwing bins, flares going off and spot fires in the street. There are cordons of riot police around.

Overall though, the heavy policing has appeared to be successful so far in staving off the type of looting, ransacking and violent activity we saw on the fringes of the marches last week. The government has added on 20% more officers, for a 70,000 strong force across the country.
Earlier today, the French interior minister had said protest numbers – at about 36,000 in the morning- were about half of what they were last Saturday.
At the Paris march, Nadège, a communications worker, said she was at Place de la République last Saturday when teargas hit. But that hadn’t deterred her.
I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now.
We have to keep our rights alive. We’ve seen what happens in the US when a bad president is in power. In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.
The French president had hosted student representatives for a highly anticipated meeting yesterday afternoon.
Going in, the student leaders had already expressed cynicism over whether the French president would adequately address their concerns.

Pupils in Paris began protests over the quality of their education four weeks ago – and their spirit has since inspired demonstrations elsewhere, across the nation and also into other countries, such as Italy and Greece.
French high schoolers say they’re fed up with the deteriorating state of their school buildings, overworked and underpaid teachers, and packed classrooms.

They’re demanding school renovations and upgrades, better study conditions and the scrapping of the Parcoursup univeristy admissions platform which was introduced in 2018 and has long been criticised for lack of transparency.
Macron held a two-and-a-half hours-long meeting with 20 students.

Nathanael Combary, president of campaign group High School Renewal, said the president had been “attentive” and they would continue talks with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Monday on proposed changes like reform of Parcoursup.
But he and other student leaders called on their peers to continue protesting this weekend.
The radical-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the La France Insoumise party, is also marching in the Parisian procession.
Speaking to the press earlier he said the protests would continue every week until Emmanuel Macron and his government addressed the public’s demands.
He said Macron “is going to understand that this is going to repeat itself every week” and urged the president, “there is still time for him to concede” to the students’ wishes.
Macron met with student leaders on Friday for the first time since the demonstrations began a month ago. More on that meeting next.
My colleague Angelique Chrisafis has been at Place d’Italie in the French capital.
Many cardboard signs held by demonstrators in Paris referenced the dozens of ongoing inquiries into mutilations and injuries by police weapons in the four weeks since high school protests began.

One 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is currently blockaded by demonstrators, said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.”
The thousands gathered in the French capital have begun walking along the designated 1.5km route from Porte d’Italie to Porte de Vincennes.
The metro trains headed to the 13th arrondisement starting point were packed.
The march has been organised by a coalition of unions, the CGT, CFDT, FSU, and Solidaires, supporting student federations, and there are the flags and banners of these various grooups.
But there are also protesters of all stripes – many young people, but also families, office workers, retirees.
Thousands of retired people and others also marched in the Spanish capital, Madrid, on Saturday, to demand that state pensions should be protected.

Pensions have become a key battleground ahead of next month’s snap election, with the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, arguing that the conservative opposition Popular party wants to privatise pensions.

Weapons confiscated included metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, Nuñez said. He added that, so far, “there has been no major incident”.

Demonstrators are on the move in Orléans, where Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party is holding its congress.

Fundamentally, systemd-nspawn is a lightweight Linux namespaces-based
container technology, not dissimilar to Docker. The difference is
mostly in image management—instead of describing how to build images with
Dockerfiles and distributing prebuilt, read-only images containing
ready-to-run software, systemd-nspawn is typically used with a writable root
filesystem, functioning more similarly to a virtual machine. For those of you
who remember using chroot to run software on a different Linux
distro, it can also be described as chroot on steroids.
I find systemd-nspawn especially useful in the following scenarios:
- When you want to run some software with some degree of isolation on a VPS, where you can’t create a full virtual machine due to nested virtualization not being available1;
- When you need to share access to hardware, such as a GPU (which is why I run
- When you don’t want the overhead of virtualization;
- When you want to directly access some files on the host system without
- When you would normally use Docker but can’t or don’t want to. For reasons, please see the footnote-turned-blog post.
In this post, I’ll describe the process of setting up systemd-nspawn
containers and how to use them in some common scenarios.

Ladies, would you get it on with a man-shaped wicker basket? He’s never heard of podcasts. You won’t have to cook for him. He has a stiff and pleasing, uh, log. But on the other hand, he is highly flammable. In early August, the indie studio Black Bear released the racy trailer for Wicker, a surrealist comedy about a spinster fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who finally gets her dream husband (Alexander Skarsgård) — one woven from willow. Online, human women reacted with a resounding and unexpected moan. They pronounced themselves proud harlots of HomeGoods, sisters in splinters. As one Instagram commenter poetically put it, “Mr. Wicker can snap, crackle, and pop this back to oblivion.” Responding to overwhelming demand, Black Bear agreed to a one-night-only 4DX screening of Wicker — personal vibrators not needed.

After years of wish-fulfillment fantasies about men falling for sex-bot companions, women are flipping the script on objectification. Wicker, based on Ursula Wills-Jones’s 2008 short story “The Wicker Husband,” is the most mainstream entry in the burgeoning category of modern romances between woman and thing. In 2017, the publishing house New Directions reissued Mrs. Caliban, Rachel Ingalls’s 1982 novella about a neglected housewife who has an affair with a fugitive amphibian; the next year, Guillermo del Toro explored a similar narrative in his film The Shape of Water. Two years after that, the movie Jumbo depicted an amusement-park worker attracted to a ride she cleans, and Julia Ducournau’s Titane, about a showgirl who has dangerous sex with a car at a motor show, won the Palme d’Or at Cannes in 2021. Recent years have brought a Noah’s ark of strange literary fiction involving trees, planes, blobs, pangolins, and soon towers — not to mention an ever-expanding universe of monster and “sentient object” smut. “Human hasn’t worked out great for me,” a baker confesses to her shiny new countertop appliance in Krista LaRae’s Creamed by My Monster Stand Mixer, after he scrambles her insides in a way no male Homo sapien has done before.

Imagine being a misogynist who believes women should stay in the kitchen only to discover that the stand mixer stole your girl! These absurdist romances, which overwhelmingly pair human women with male creatures and objects, infuse levity into the depressing topic of modern (heterosexual) love. (Queers seeking representation should search for Chuck Tingle, sentient-object legend behind gems like My Macaroni and Cheese Is a Lesbian Also She Is My Lawyer and Pounded in the Butt by My Hugo Award Loss.) The stories also match these debauched, stranger-than-fiction times. Just last month, FBI director Kash Patel defended the agency’s decision to remove “bestiality” as an automatic hiring disqualifier, to the surprise of flabbergasted members of Congress. One (debunked, but who’s to say) rumor about Vice-President J.D. Vance is that he once fornicated with a couch. What else do you expect from a far-right administration that preaches “family values” while overrun with perverts?

Wicker is perfectly calibrated for our moment of peak heteropessimism. In the film, gender is depicted as a binary. Marriage is quite literally imprisonment; wedding ceremonies conclude with the groom locking his new wife into a metal collar. The Fisherwoman, Wicker’s spinster protagonist, is self-sufficient but lonely, bullied by townspeople for remaining single. Desperate for acceptance, she pleads for the local basket weaver (Peter Dinklage) to make her a husband. He obliges, and the wicker husband lumbers into the church to say “I do” a month later.

The husband is not human but undoubtedly a man. He is over six feet tall, chiseled, and skilled at manual labor. He is not socialized enough to understand patriarchy but somehow has the expert ability to make women come. (It also helps that he’s played by a svelte Skarsgård.) Ultimately, what Wicker has to say about gender is not particularly novel. More interesting is what it might lay bare about the challenges of being a real person today.

Wicker takes place loosely during the medieval era, before the rise of capitalism and what the social scientist Max Weber once referred to as the “disenchantment of the world.” A modern tale like Agnieszka Szpila’s Hexes of the Deadwood Forest conveys how even when women win under the status quo, they lose. It follows Anna Frenza, the ruthless CEO of Poland’s biggest oil company. A cartoon villain, she lives in a wealthy neighborhood where the decomposed bodies of the poor fertilize the gardens of the rich. She couldn’t care less about climate change; she won’t suffer the consequences. Still, she is not happy. Her husband, Bartek, was disabled in a car accident, so she must take care of him while working. Sex is practically nonexistent in their marriage, though even when they did have it she felt dehumanized by it: “She craved sex that involved a mindful connection, built on intimacy — but Bartek reacted as if someone were puking in his face at the mere sound of the word ‘intimacy.’” Anna wanted to be a partner, not a dominatrix.

Hexes takes “touch grass” to more scandalous ends. Anna self-medicates with wine and lithium. One day, in a druggy trance, she sleepwalks into the forest, where a journey catches her having sex with a fallen tree (and specifically lesbian sex, it seems): “As she licks the drops of resin that are oozing from the slit in the tree’s trunk, she shares her own moisture with it. So that she’s not just taking but exchanging mutually.” She’s thrown out as CEO, just another failed diversity corporate experiment. Descending into madness, she mentally transports to the 17th century, where she encounters a women-only commune that advocates for the rejection of patriarchy and literally orgasmic embrace of Mother Earth.

This type of back-to-the-land, pussy-power politics is dangerous, relying on a gender essentialism that’s easily co-opted by tradwives and other conservatives. Wouldn’t it be nice to bake bread all day and retreat into your “divine feminine”? But it speaks to a collective feeling of crisis, the wish to reverse time to escape what we’re told is an inevitable future: climate catastrophe, extreme wealth inequality, and complete takeover by AI. Wicker’s premodern setting is undoubtedly part of its charm, too — there are artisans, town gathering spaces, and unspoiled nature. All it needs are women’s rights.

In the modern day, violence against women is obscured, “buried in layers of hierarchy and consumerism, where the potential of using it belongs almost exclusively to powerful men,” a sentient printer says in Fien Veldman’s Hard Copy. The printer is the unnamed office-worker protagonist’s only friend. The worker moves from a blue-collar town to the big city, supposedly an escape from a rough upbringing. But the city is no paradise. Her company pays her minimum wage minus the cost of her lunch. The unnamed worker has an autoimmune disease that flares up when she exerts herself too much — an epidemic among young women, according to her allergist. Exploiting this, a male co-worker intentionally sends her on a goose chase to find a package so he can claim her office. Unwell, she is put on leave. Her kinship with the printer makes sense: To their office, both of them are disposable objects.

Those who aren’t ejected from the workplace must try to stay afloat. In Ana Paula Pacheco’s Pandora, Ana, a literature professor in São Paulo, is broke after getting hospitalized from COVID. The novel begins with a loopy account of her falling in love with a pangolin. She quarantines with him, relieved to have someone else to help with household chores, but he grows abusive and eventually rapes her. Later, she takes a bat as a lover who insists on leaving the carcasses of his prey in the apartment while insects and vermin swarm the ground. These appear to be allegories for the brutality of COVID; both pangolins and bats were early carriers of the disease. We learn that Ana’s ex-girlfriend passed away, and perhaps this is Ana processing grief. She morphs too; in the book’s most disturbing scene, she is a dolphin undergoing labiaplasty to restore her once-smooth skin. Youth is currency, and she turns to sex work to make money for her kids.

To function, Ana takes Wellbutrin. Her male psychiatrist dismisses her rants and simply urges her to be patient with her medication. He responds to her grief with cold pragmatism: “He asks why I don’t reactivate my Tinder account instead of dwelling on what I’ve lost,” Ana says. The fact that Hexes of the Deadwood Forest, Hard Copy, and Pandora all feature women going mad is not a coincidence. They illustrate that mental-health crises aren’t anomalies, but an inevitable byproduct of a horrifying system. Drugs and distractions are needed to blur out reality: If you can see the world clearly, how could you not be depressed?

If some nonhuman love interests are imagined symbols of distress, others are convenient justifications for avoiding other, presumably more socially adept humans. The protagonist of Kate Folk’s Sky Daddy, Linda, is a 30-year-old content moderator who filters hate and harassment on a video-sharing platform, thus training the company’s AI algorithm to eventually take her place. She forages office snacks for meals and lives in relative squalor in a windowless room in a basement. She has only one friend, her co-worker Karina. No matter; by then she’ll be betrothed to her soon-to-be husband, a Boeing 737.

Sky Daddy subverts the traditional marriage plot: Linda’s grand journey to find love is really a suicide quest. Linda’s sexual interest in planes began when she was 13 after a flight to Chicago on a 737 named N92823. The plane hit turbulence and dropped 50 feet. “I was filled with a warm liquid sensation, a feeling of inevitability, along with wave upon wave of pleasure, what I would later understand had been my first orgasm,” she recalls. “I wanted the turbulence to go on and on, to build to a climax, the plane diving nose-first into the earth. A perfect death!” Relationships complicate this goal: Growing to care about Karina prompts Linda to care for herself too. Embarrassed to be eating too much of Karina’s food, Linda starts to buy real groceries. Karina buys her the first gift she can remember receiving: a seasonal depression lamp for her room. When Linda blows her money chasing N92823, only to be “rejected” by him, it is Karina who comes running through the airport to rescue her, despite her fear of flights. “None of that matters to me,” she says about Linda’s sexual preferences. “The important thing is, you’ve always been a good friend.”

Maggie Su’s Blob, meanwhile, is a twist on the classic Build-a-Boy story. Outside of a dive bar, a loner named Vi encounters a “beige gelatin splotch the size of a dinner plate.” He is a blob that she names Bob and carries home. Vi is in limbo: She dropped out of college after flunking her biomedical-engineering class and now works reception at a hotel in her town. She is single after being dumped by her ex-boyfriend, a guy whom her brother called “the most generic white man in the world” but to her is proof that she’ll never be loved. Bob is a chance to do it over. The formless entity sprouts limbs and facial features. She feeds him ’90s sitcoms, Jeopardy!, and printed photos of young George Clooney, and he evolves into a dream man.

But as Bob finally becomes a person, he begins to rebel and flees. “I should’ve anticipated that molding him into a man would trigger something deeper, some sort of existential awakening. Now he’s just like everyone else,” Vi laments. It isn’t Bob who is amorphous, but Vi. “All the mistakes I made because I wanted to prove to myself what I never fully believed: that I belonged, that I was worthy. I struck out before I could get rejected or forced someone to reject me so I could leave on my terms,” she says. Over the course of the book, her personality sharpens. She picks up photography, reenrolls in school, and opens herself to dating again. It’s only through friction with other people that you come to find yourself, Blob emphasizes.

Wicker does not lead you to the same conclusions. The Fisherwoman is a blank character. We know little about her besides that she’s an orphan with no family or friends. She is supposedly the sole reason for the wicker husband’s existence, yet the movie also attempts to emphasize that he had the agency to pick her over everyone else. When she asks the basket maker whether her husband truly loves her, he scoffs, “Pardon me, I did not build some fuckable furniture. If he said he loved you, it’s true.” The film wants to satisfy conflicting desires: not to have to choose while being chosen yourself, to being loved without truly known.

There is also no real attempt in the film to explore how her life might have been transformed by friends, what would have happened had she perhaps united with her fellow women. (It does at least depict the local tailor’s wife eventually leaving her husband to forge a life of her own.) In the end, the basket weaver, the Fisherwoman, and her husband ride off into the sunset, to a new society, while the wretched stay behind. Wicker is, ultimately, a fairy tale. But in real life, there’s no fade to black or happy ending. We have to continue living. We have to write the next chapter ourselves.

The term carpetbagger was originally applied to Northerners who moved South after the Civil War to launch political careers under the protection of military Reconstruction; it referred to the hastily procured bags manufactured from carpet scraps the transplants allegedly used. More recently, the term has been applied to politicians who conveniently relocate themselves into the vicinity of political opportunities. New York has often been a magnet for alleged carpetbaggers. In the 1960s alone, two former U.S. attorneys general, Robert F. Kennedy and Ramsey Clark, moved to the Empire State and ran for the Senate (the former successfully, the latter not so much), and a generation later, so did former Arkansas First Lady Hillary Clinton (like RFK, she won).

So in itself, the decision by conservative ex-lobbyist and businessman Zach Lahn to move from Kansas to Iowa in 2024 and then run for governor — winning the 2026 GOP primary in a big upset — isn’t so remarkable. Indeed, Lahn was born and grew up in Iowa, where his family had lived for generations, and owned property there.

What has made his case interesting — and for supporters of his Democratic opponent, Rob Sand, hilarious — is his difficulty making a clean break with it. He seems very involved in Kansas matters. He remains president of the board of an unaccredited Wichita private school he co-founded with his wife, albeit when they were both married to other people (in her case to a scion of the Kansas Koch family empire, with whom she financed the Wonder School, as they called it). And the children from the blended families he and his wife left in Kansas have given Lahn a reason to fly his private plane back to Wichita a lot — at least 37 times since he began running for governor, according to the Des Moines Register. But that isn’t the only evidence that Lahn has Kansas on his mind. Last month, the Daily Beast reported that a Strava fitness-app user with the name “Zach Lahn” recorded four long bike rides starting at Lahn’s Wichita estate over three months in early 2025, long after his supposed relocation to Iowa.

Perhaps more eyebrow-raising have been his public musings over the amount of time he’ll need to spend away from Iowa’s capital if he does become the governor of the Hawkeye State. “We’ve already had discussions about this and how that would work,” he told the Register in May. “But if I’m elected governor, it would be a different arrangement, and we’d work it out. Because, you know, we’d be in Iowa as much as humanly possible.”

That has to be comforting, but it certainly hasn’t quelled questions about Lahn’s state loyalties, considering his campaign’s Trump-modeled message is “Iowa First.” Or at least since October 17, 2024, which was when he transferred his voter registration to the state. You’re required to have Iowa residency for at least two years to run for governor there, so he got in just under the wire.
Unsurprisingly, Lahn’s shaky status as an Iowan has been bread and meat for Sand’s campaign, which has offered him Iowa travel tips:
And even more cleverly, Sand’s backers got Kansas’s Democratic governor Laura Kelly in on the action:

When Lahn first decided to run, his “outsider” status might have seemed like a positive credential. The current two-term Republican governor of Iowa, Kim Reynolds, is deeply unpopular (for many months, she’s reigned as “America’s most unpopular governor” according to polling from Morning Consult). So while he was campaigning in the primary against Iowa GOP Establishment candidate Randy Feenstra, Lahn made a logical choice by separating himself from the usual suspects in Des Moines and Washington. But Wichita is a little too “outside” Iowa for comfort. And in explaining the details of his family situation, Lahn has also drawn attention to his not entirely orthodox relationship with the insanely rich and controversial Koch family (for whom he worked as an Americans for Prosperity operative before marrying Chase Koch’s ex-wife). He’s not just any old dad with custody issues.

Other than the poor management of his residential status, Lahn was unlucky to have made his move back to Iowa for what is turning out to be a strong Democratic year in a state that turned deep red in 2014 and has remained so ever since. Democrats have even odds of winning the Senate seat being vacated by Joni Ernst and could flip three of Iowa’s four U.S. House seats as well. In Sand, the sole member of his party in statewide office, Democrats have a solidly established centrist candidate who is difficult for the GOP to label as a “radical” or “socialist” (though it has tried). Lahn has sought to adopt a populist stance by criticizing both major party establishments and has a MAHA strain in his ideology that has enabled him to attack polluters with whom Republicans often snuggle. The two candidates are more or less evenly matched financially.

In part because of a vast advantage in name ID, Sand has led Lahn in public polling from the get-go. In the Silver Bulletin polling averages, Sand leads by a robust 7.3 percent, though the most recent polls show the race tightening a bit. As in other midwestern states, Democrats are nervous about possible polling errors (Iowa is, after all, where the legendary pollster Ann Selzer infamously showed Kamala Harris leading Trump in 2024). The Trump administration, meanwhile, is working overtime to deliver tasty treats (e.g., fuel assistance to hard-pressed farmers and a new federally assisted steel mill) to Iowa voters.

If Sand nonetheless prevails, Republicans will naturally wonder if a more Iowa-centric candidate like Feenstra might have won. And Lahn may wonder whether he picked the wrong “home state” for his gubernatorial dreams.

The Indiana Fever are undergoing a major front-office shakeup. President of basketball and business operations Kelly Krauskopf has stepped down and general manager Amber Cox has been fired. The team announced Krauskopf's decision to step away on Friday morning before later announcing Cox's departure.

Krauskopf was the Fever's original president and general manager for their inaugural season in 2000, and remained in that role until 2018, when the Indiana Pacers hired her as their assistant general manager and she became the first woman in NBA history to hold an executive basketball management role. During her first stint with the Fever, Krauskopf built one of the most consistent organizations in the league. The Fever made the playoffs 13 times in her 19 seasons, including 12 consecutive seasons from 2005-16, which remains a WNBA record. Under Krauskopf's leadership, the Fever won their first and only title in 2012, and also reached the Finals in 2009 and 2015.

Krauskopf returned to the Fever in 2024 and was part of the organization's decision to hire Cox as chief operating officer and general manager. That was the same year Caitlin Clark arrived and the franchise's worldwide popularity exploded. The Fever made the playoffs in each of the last three seasons, but never advanced past the semifinals, and Krauskopf and Cox have both faced criticism for failing to build a better team around Clark, Aliyah Boston, and Kelsey Mitchell.

The organizational shakeup comes as an important offseason for the franchise is underway. Mitchell is an unrestricted free agent, but now the Fever are without a president and general manager. Krauskopf informed the organization of her decision prior to the end of the season, so you'd assume the organization has been working on a succession plan, but the Fever will need to make some decisions quickly.
This is a critical offseason for the franchise, and whoever replaces Krauskopf and Cox will immediately be thrown into the fire.
Why is this such an important offseason for the Fever?

After a first-round exit to the Las Vegas Aces, the Fever have some major items on the agenda this offseason. First and foremost, they want to re-sign Mitchell, who is an unrestricted free agent. Cox said Mitchell will be a "major priority," and it's fair to assume the new front office will feel the same way. Clark, for her part, said that she and her teammates will recruit Mitchell "as hard as we can."
Mitchell, however, is unsure of her future with the Fever, who drafted her No. 2 overall back in 2018.

"I have to be selfish," Mitchell said during her exit interview. "I think that's where I am in my career ... what I probably need and what's probably best for me. So I have to be selfish in that room. "But I think, ultimately, being on the Fever and being a part of an organization that does come with a lot of ups and downs, what factors in and what is important for me is, obviously, having a good chemistry on and off the floor. I've only been with one team my entire career, so it's all kind of like figuring this out. It's hard, man."

Clark, meanwhile, is eligible for an EPIC (Exceptional Performance on Initial Contract) extension, which allows players to renegotiate the fourth year of their rookie contract and sign a three-year extension. During her exit interview, Clark hinted at being willing to take a discount, but did not say whether she'll sign an EPIC deal.
"I think for myself, my focus is on winning. I certainly know what I deserve and what I'm worth, but at the same time, sometimes you have to make sacrifices," Clark said.

The Mitchell and Clark contract decisions will complicate an already messy cap sheet for the Fever. Even if both were willing to take a slight discount to return, the Fever would still have three players -- including Boston, who signed an EPIC extension last offseason -- taking up about 60% of the salary cap moving forward, and it's not easy to build a championship roster with so few resources for everyone else. That's especially true when the Fever still have Monique Billings and Lexie Hull on the books for $800K apiece next season -- the result of a pair of disastrous deals Krauskopf and Cox handed out last offseason.
Stephanie White expected to remain as coach

Ahead of the 2025 season, Krauskopf and Cox fired coach Christie Sides and replaced her with the veteran Stephanie White, who played for the Fever from 2000-04 and previously served as an assistant coach from 2011-14 and head coach from 2015-16. White has one year remaining on her contract and is expected to remain in her role, according to The Athletic.

White has made the playoffs in each of her two seasons in charge, and the Fever's 24 wins this season were a franchise record. However, the team has not advanced past the semifinals, and White has faced steady criticism for how she's handled Clark and the team overall.
Clark has routinely backed White, though, and did so again at her exit interview.

"I really appreciate Steph. I like to say this is the best job in women's basketball and possibly women's sports, getting to lead this franchise that has so much notoriety, but at the same time, it can come with some negatives and people are gonna criticize everything that you can do. That's just the reality, people expect greatness," Clark said.

"Personally, my relationship with Steph, she's somebody that's always supported me. It's been really fun getting to play for her," Clark continued. "She just tries to win, she's competitive. She expects great things out of us. She has a fiery passion about her that I really, really admire. I think I have a lot of that in myself too. One of my most special memories of this year is getting to win a gold medal with her in Berlin. That's not something anybody can ever take away from us."
New front office has work to do to repair reputation

During Game 2 of the Fever's first-round series with the Aces, MVP A'ja Wilson confronted a fan sitting along the baseline, who she felt had been disrespectful. Wilson received a technical foul for the incident, which became a national talking point and reignited the discourse about Fever fans and the organization's reputation.
During her exit interview, Cox said that "attacks on our fanbase have no basis in reality, and they need to stop.

"Every organization in the league, every organization throughout professional sports, all the way down to youth rec leagues, have to deal with occasional bad behavior from spectators. And anyone who crosses the line in an arena or online needs to be held accountable. I want to be really clear about that. There is a line, and people need to be held accountable if they cross it," Cox said.

"But here's the fact: We did not have one fan pointed out by a player who violated the WNBA code of conduct this season. Not one fan was removed from a game. ... Our fans love this team. They're going to cheer, they're going to boo, and sometimes they might point. It's a home-court advantage for a reason, and it's the same for the Pacers. And all of that is within the code of conduct."
That same day, however, Mitchell admitted that she didn't always enjoy playing in front of Fever fans.

"Showing up every day to compete for fans that may or may not like you is hard," Mitchell said. "I think this organization is unbelievable, man, but I think that when it comes to, like, really trying to be yourself, it hasn't always been easy."

Early on Friday, prior to the changes in the Fever's front office, The Athletic published a report in which one agent said that multiple of their clients had been called the N-word in Indianapolis. And earlier this season, Alyssa Thomas and DeWanna Bonner said they received death threats and had their addresses leaked after Thomas was retroactively assessed a Flagrant 2 foul and suspended for one game following an in-game altercation with Clark.

During her exit interview, Clark once again denounced fans who use her name for the wrong reasons. "As far as people that have used me to demonstrate racist rhetoric or hate or discrimination, that's not something I stand for," Clark said. "That's never been something I've stood for. For those of you that know me, that's not what I'm about, that's not how I was raised, so that's really disappointing when people do that."
In addition to recruiting Mitchell and figuring out Clark's extension, the Fever's new front office will have to repair the franchise's reputation around the league.
